findings.quote: **Double jeopardy** protects a person from being placed in jeopardy of punishment twice for the same offense after the first criminal case has reached the kind of result protected by law.
findings.problem: The phrase "the kind of result protected by law" is left undefined, so the general double-jeopardy rule is not taught well enough for a learner to know when the first case creates the protection. The later worked case covers only the special law-and-ordinance situation.

checked: Checked stated conditions and exceptions for political-belief detention, involuntary servitude, debt, ex post facto laws, and bills of attainder; the general double-jeopardy applicability conditions remain unstated.

findings.quote: The Constitution also gives a special rule when the same act is punished by both a law and an ordinance. A conviction or acquittal under either one bars another prosecution for the same act under the other.
findings.problem: This states the special law-and-ordinance condition, but the lesson never states the relevant conditions for the general same-offense double-jeopardy protection. Without those limits, the learner cannot tell when the general rule applies.

lesson-philippine-constitution-bill-of-r.quote: > Section $18$ does not say that political beliefs excuse an unrelated crime.
lesson-philippine-constitution-bill-of-r.note: The required General Information Traps section is now present; Speed Tricks is optional under the supplied ruling.

lesson-philippine-constitution-bill-of-r.quote: An **ex post facto law** is a penal rule that works backward in a way that harms the accused.
lesson-philippine-constitution-bill-of-r.note: The rewrite now gives plain local meanings for ex post facto law, bill of attainder, double jeopardy, involuntary servitude, and poll tax before they are applied.

general-information-philippine-constitut.quote: Article III, Section $18$ says that a person cannot be detained only because of political beliefs or aspirations.
general-information-philippine-constitut.note: The rewrite now states the political-belief detention protection and applies it in the first worked example.

general-information-philippine-constitut.quote: Section $18$ also bans **involuntary servitude**, which means being forced to work or serve against one's will. The Constitution allows an exception when the service is punishment for a crime after due conviction.
general-information-philippine-constitut.note: The rewrite now explains involuntary servitude and the due-conviction exception, then applies that exception in a worked example.

general-information-philippine-constitut.quote: Section $19$ bans excessive fines. It also bans cruel, degrading, or inhuman punishment.
general-information-philippine-constitut.note: The rewrite now explicitly teaches the excessive-fines protection and adds a worked excessive-fine scenario.

general-information-philippine-constitut.quote: Section $19$ bans excessive fines. It also bans cruel, degrading, or inhuman punishment.
general-information-philippine-constitut.note: The rewrite now teaches the cruel, degrading, or inhuman punishment protection and applies degrading punishment in the rights-analysis example.

general-information-philippine-constitut.quote: **Double jeopardy** protects a person from being placed in jeopardy of punishment twice for the same offense after the first criminal case has reached the kind of result protected by law.
general-information-philippine-constitut.note: The rewrite now states the same-offense principle and separately teaches the law-and-ordinance conviction/acquittal rule requested by the brief.

general-information-philippine-constitut.quote: An **ex post facto law** is a penal rule that works backward in a way that harms the accused.
general-information-philippine-constitut.note: The rewrite now explains the harmful retroactive penal idea and applies it to a later harsher punishment.

general-information-philippine-constitut.quote: A **bill of attainder** is a legislative act that punishes a named person or group without a judicial trial.
general-information-philippine-constitut.note: The rewrite now gives the meaning and a direct application involving punishment by Congress without judicial trial.

general-information-philippine-constitut.quote: Start with the facts. Identify what government action happened, which right may apply, and whether the Constitution states an exception or condition.
general-information-philippine-constitut.note: The rewrite now teaches an evidence-based analysis sequence and applies it to degrading punishment of a detainee.

general-information-philippine-constitut.quote: Human-rights violations can cause loss of liberty, unfair punishment, fear, and loss of trust in public institutions. They can also harm families and communities.
general-information-philippine-constitut.note: The rewrite now explains personal and social effects instead of only listing constitutional protections.

general-information-philippine-constitut.quote: Protection methods depend on the facts. A person may seek legal help and the proper court remedy.
general-information-philippine-constitut.note: The rewrite now teaches legal-help and court-remedy paths and also explains the Commission on Human Rights investigation and legal-aid role.
